notes.send_advice: Replace "Mars rocks on Earth (~175)" with "Mars rocks on Earth (roughly 400 known)" or drop the number entirely; the Meteoritical Bulletin lists 366 approved shergottites alone and USRA gives about 400 Martian meteorites as of August 2026. The Moon clause can stay as it is hedged, or be dropped since Hank's Moon sentence is not wrong.
notes.reason: This is Hank's own scripted narration, not a guest's or a quoted source's: "we know that rocks travel between planets because there's Mars rocks on Earth and there's Earth rocks on Mars." The caption cannot have misheard it, because the sentence is a deliberate mirror (Mars rocks on Earth, Earth rocks on Mars) and the next sentence, "We found Earth rocks on the moon," shows he means literal finds. The correction holds up: every meteorite identified on Mars by a rover (Heat Shield Rock, Block Island, the 2025 Perseverance candidate Phippsaksla) is an iron-nickel asteroidal body, the note's geology.com source says exactly what the accepted quotes claim, and I found no paper or press release claiming an Earth-origin rock on Mars. It matters to his point, since he presents the Earth-rocks-on-Mars find as one of only two pieces of evidence that rocks cross between planets, and a viewer would come away believing it happened. Hank corrects himself readily and this is a plain factual slip, so he would likely accept it. The flaw is inside the note: the parenthetical count of about 175 Mars rocks on Earth is wrong and unsourced (the Meteoritical Bulletin database shows 366 approved shergottites alone and USRA cites about 400 Martian meteorites in August 2026), so that clause must be fixed before sending. The Moon clause is hedged and consistent with the Apollo 14 Big Bertha result, so it is not disqualifying.
